📚 Reference Links

  • What Ingress specifies, and what it leaves to annotations — Kubernetes: Ingress

  • The controller half of the contract — Kubernetes: Ingress Controllers

  • The role-separated successor API — Gateway API: Introduction

  • Sidecar and sidecarless data planes — Istio: Sidecar or ambient?

  • Bonus — Envoy: Life of a Request

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which direction does each handle? Ingress and Gateway: north-south. Mesh: east-west. They compose, not compete.
Why did Gateway API replace Ingress? Ingress specified only host and path; everything else became unportable vendor annotations.
The three Gateway API roles? GatewayClass (infra provider), Gateway (cluster operator), Route (app developer).
What does a mesh give that a gateway cannot? Policy on service-to-service traffic that never passes through the edge — plus workload-identity mTLS.
The anti-pattern to name? Hairpinning east-west traffic out to the ingress and back in.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

These are three layers, not three options. Ingress is the original north-south API: host and path routing to Services, with everything else — buffering, timeouts, rewrites — expressed as per-controller annotations, which is exactly why it is being replaced. Gateway API is the successor: the same job with those features typed rather than stringly, and split across three roles so a platform team owns the Gateway while application teams own their own Routes. A service mesh handles east-west instead: mTLS, retries and per-request balancing between services, which never touches the edge. A mature cluster runs a gateway and a mesh, and the interesting question is where each responsibility sits.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How do a gateway and a mesh actually compose on one request path?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can trace a request across both without them overlapping incoherently.

An external request arrives at a cloud load balancer pointing at the gateway's Service, and the gateway — an in-cluster proxy — terminates TLS, matches the request against its Route rules and selects a backend. If a mesh is present, the gateway is usually itself part of it, so instead of dialling a ClusterIP it dials the destination workload's pod addresses over mTLS, and the destination's sidecar terminates that connection and hands the request to the application on loopback.

From there, every subsequent hop is east-west and the gateway is out of the picture entirely. Service A calling Service B goes A → A's sidecar → B's sidecar → B, with retries, timeouts, per-request balancing and mTLS applied by the sidecars. The gateway never sees it, which is the whole reason a mesh exists: most traffic in a microservice estate never crosses the edge, so edge policy cannot govern it.

The clean division to state out loud: the gateway owns "who may enter and where does this go", the mesh owns "how services talk to each other". Where they overlap — retries, timeouts, TLS — the rule is to configure each responsibility once, at the hop that owns it, because two layers both retrying multiplies load on a struggling backend.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Do you actually need all three?

📍 Seen in the wild: the closing question on any platform design that draws all of them.

🎯 Really testing: whether you have adoption thresholds or a reflex.

Almost nobody needs Ingress and Gateway API — those are the same layer, and running both means two routing APIs in flight and two places a route can be defined. The honest position is that new clusters start on Gateway API and established ones migrate when annotation sprawl, not feature envy, becomes the pain (Section 11, Item 117).

The gateway-versus-mesh question is genuinely separate, and the mesh is the one to justify. Its thresholds are: three or more languages, because one good client library beats a proxy hop for a homogeneous estate; a hard requirement you cannot otherwise meet, most often mTLS everywhere for compliance or per-request balancing of internal gRPC; and enough services that per-service policy is unmanageable by hand. Below those, a gateway plus client libraries is less machinery and a smaller failure domain.

My default for a platform team: Gateway API for north-south, and a mesh only when mTLS across a polyglot estate or internal gRPC balancing is already hurting — adopted in ambient mode if available, since the per-pod proxy cost is what makes meshes expensive at scale. What I would not do is adopt a mesh for observability alone; that is available more cheaply from the gateway and from eBPF tooling.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

What degrades as Route and Service counts grow across many teams?

📍 Seen in the wild: the multi-tenant platform question.

Configuration size and reload behaviour, before request throughput. An ingress controller compiles every Ingress or Route in the cluster into one proxy configuration; with thousands of routes, generating and applying that config takes seconds. Older NGINX-based controllers reloaded the whole process on any change, which reset long-lived connections cluster-wide — so one team adding a path caused every other team's WebSocket and SSE users to disconnect. Envoy-based controllers push incremental updates over xDS instead, which is the main architectural reason to prefer them at scale.

For a mesh, the equivalent is control-plane fan-out: every configuration change must be computed and pushed to every proxy, so the work scales with (config size × proxy count), and a cluster with thousands of sidecars can see propagation delays measured in tens of seconds. It presents as configuration that is applied but not yet in effect — a route change that works for some pods and not others — which is maddening to debug because both the manifest and the proxy are behaving correctly.

The signals are config-reload duration and xDS push latency on the control plane, plus connection-reset spikes correlated with unrelated teams' deploys. The remedies are an xDS-based controller rather than a reloading one, scoping mesh configuration so each proxy receives only what concerns it (Istio's Sidecar resource, or ambient mode's per-namespace proxies), and splitting very large clusters rather than growing one control plane indefinitely.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the traffic layers for a multi-tenant AI platform: browser traffic, internal gRPC, and GPU inference.

🎯 Really testing: whether you assign each responsibility to exactly one hop and can defend the placement.

The dominating constraint is that these three traffic shapes want different things, and the streaming path is the one that breaks silently. So the design assigns responsibilities rather than drawing boxes: NLB → Gateway (Gateway API) → workloads, with the gateway owning TLS termination, host and path routing, per-tenant rate limiting after auth, and — critically — response buffering off with a long timeout on the token-streaming route, because that default destroys time-to-first-token at any hop that has it (Section 11, Item 121).

East-west gets a mesh, justified specifically by internal gRPC: sidecars give per-request balancing across pods, which is what stops five callers pinning forty inference replicas (Section 11, Item 114), and they supply mTLS with workload identity for the multi-tenant requirement. Inference traffic is routed to pods individually — a headless Service or an EndpointSlice-aware gateway — with least-request and power-of-two-choices rather than round robin, because generation cost varies by orders of magnitude (Item 146). NetworkPolicy sits underneath all of it as default-deny per namespace, because the mesh authorizes but the flat network still routes (Item 143).

The failure I would monitor first is client-measured time-to-first-token on the streaming route, since every hop above can destroy it and no server-side metric shows it. Second is per-pod request distribution on the GPU fleet, the detector for pinning. Third is xDS push latency, because a mesh whose config is lagging produces route behaviour that is correct in the manifest and wrong in production — and that is the failure that costs a whole afternoon.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Ingress Gateway API Service mesh
Direction North-south North-south East-west
Routing expressiveness Host and path only, in-spec Host, path, header, method, query; weighted splits; mirroring Full L7, plus per-request policy
Everything else Vendor annotations — unvalidated strings Typed fields with schema validation CRDs per mesh
Role separation None GatewayClass / Gateway / Route Platform owns the mesh, teams own policy
mTLS between services No No Yes, with workload identity
Per-request balancing to pods Controller-dependent Yes Yes, everywhere
Protocols HTTP(S) HTTP, gRPC, TLS, TCP, UDP Whatever the proxy supports
Cost A controller A controller A proxy per pod (or per node in ambient) plus a control plane
When you'd actually pick it Existing clusters, simple exposure New clusters, multi-team ownership Polyglot estate needing mTLS or internal gRPC balancing

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The layers do not overlap in the datapath; they overlap in policy. Both a gateway and a mesh can retry, time out and terminate TLS, and configuring the same behaviour twice is where the failures live: two hops each retrying three times is nine attempts against a struggling backend, and an inner timeout longer than an outer one means the outer hop reports a 504 that names the wrong culprit. The design rule is one owner per responsibility.

Config propagation is the scaling term, not request throughput. A gateway compiles all Routes into one proxy configuration; a mesh pushes configuration to every proxy. The first scales with route count, the second with (config size × proxy count). Both present the same way — configuration applied but not yet in effect — and neither shows up in request-path metrics.

The mesh's per-hop cost is two proxy traversals per call. At a few hundred microseconds each that is negligible against a 40ms backend and material against a 2ms cache lookup, so the cost lands hardest on the chattiest, fastest calls. Across a fan-out of n services, tail-latency amplification applies: the chance that no hop is slow falls as p^n, so a fan-out's p99 degrades faster than any single hop's.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This is where the difference between a cluster and a platform shows. Ingress plus a controller gets traffic in; a gateway with typed routes and role separation lets ten teams change their own routing without a shared config file; a mesh makes "all internal traffic is encrypted and retried consistently" a property of the platform rather than of each team's diligence.

The observable that matters most is config propagation latency — reload duration for a gateway, xDS push latency for a mesh. It is the number that decides whether a route change takes effect in one second or forty, and it is the root of the most confusing class of incident in this area: manifests that are correct and behaviour that is not.

The second is connection resets correlated with unrelated teams' deploys. On a reloading ingress controller this is the signature that one team's route change is disconnecting another team's streaming users, and it is invisible unless you look for the correlation.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Gateway API: the platform team owns the Gateway and its TLS
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: { name: edge, namespace: infra }
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: https
      port: 443
      protocol: HTTPS
      tls: { certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-cert }] }
      allowedRoutes: { namespaces: { from: Selector, selector: { matchLabels: { gateway-access: "true" } } } }
---
# The application team owns its own Route, in its own namespace
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: chat, namespace: team-ai }
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: edge, namespace: infra }]
  hostnames: ["chat.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1/stream } }]
      timeouts: { request: 0s }        # TYPED field - was an unvalidated annotation under Ingress
      backendRefs: [{ name: chat, port: 8080 }]
    - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /v1/ } }]
      backendRefs:
        - { name: chat, port: 8080, weight: 90 }
        - { name: chat-canary, port: 8080, weight: 10 }   # weighted split, also typed

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The Gateway above, in a cluster with a mesh, serving a streaming request and then an internal call.

📥 [1] browser → NLB → gateway pod  ................................ source IP preserved
    │
    ▼
🔒 [2] gateway terminates TLS, matches HTTPRoute /v1/stream
    │   timeouts.request: 0s → no request timeout on the streaming route
    │   buffering off → tokens forwarded as produced (Section 11, Item 121)
    ▼
🛡️ [3] gateway dials a POD address over mTLS, not the ClusterIP
    │   ← this is what makes per-request balancing possible for HTTP/2
    ▼
⚙️ [4] chat pod emits first SSE frame at t+190ms → forwarded immediately
    │   client TTFT ~195ms ✅  (with buffering on anywhere: ~8s)
    ▼
🔁 [5] chat → embeddings, east-west. Gateway NEVER involved.
    │   sidecar A → sidecar B, mTLS, least-request across B's 12 pods
    ▼
📊 [6] per-request choice: max/median in-flight per pod ≈ 1.1
    │   through a ClusterIP instead, 1 connection would pin all of it to 1 pod
    ▼
⚠️ [7] a second team applies an unrelated HTTPRoute
    │   xDS incremental push → ~1.2s to take effect, NO connection resets
    │   (a reloading NGINX controller here would have reset every open stream)

  1. Step 2's typed timeout is the Gateway API argument in one line. Under Ingress this was nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600" — an unvalidated string, silently ignored if misspelled, and meaningless to any other controller. Here it is a schema-validated field.

  2. Step 3 bypasses the ClusterIP deliberately. Dialling pod addresses is what lets the gateway make a per-request decision; going through a Service would hand the choice to kube-proxy, which makes it once per connection (Item 139).

  3. Step 5 is the whole case for a mesh. This call never approaches the edge, so no amount of gateway configuration governs it. mTLS, retries and per-request balancing here are properties of the mesh or of nothing.

  4. Step 6 is the metric that proves it. 1.1 max-to-median means the twelve pods are genuinely sharing work; the same call through a ClusterIP with one HTTP/2 connection would show one pod at 100% and eleven idle, with zero errors anywhere.

  5. Step 7 is the scaling property people discover late. Incremental xDS pushes mean another team's route change costs ~1.2 seconds of propagation and no disruption. On a controller that reloads its whole process, that same change resets every long-lived connection in the cluster — which is a cross-team outage caused by a routine deploy.

10. When TO Use This

  • Gateway API for north-south on any new cluster. Typed features, role separation, and protocol coverage beyond HTTP make it the better starting point even before annotation sprawl appears.

  • Ingress where it already works and the annotation set is small. Migration has a cost; pay it when portability or multi-team ownership starts to hurt, not on principle.

  • A mesh when mTLS across a polyglot estate is a requirement, or when internal gRPC balancing is already causing idle replicas. Those two justify it; observability alone does not.

  • Ambient or sidecarless mode where available, because per-pod proxy overhead is the cost that makes meshes expensive at a thousand pods.

  • All three layers together on a mature platform — gateway for entry, mesh for east-west, NetworkPolicy underneath — with each responsibility owned by exactly one of them.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not run Ingress and Gateway API for the same traffic. They are the same layer; two routing APIs means two places a route can be defined and two mental models for on-call to hold.

  • Do not hairpin east-west traffic through the ingress. Service-to-service calls leaving the cluster network and coming back add latency, a shared failure domain and a bill, for policy a mesh or a client library would apply in place.

  • Do not adopt a mesh for a small, single-language estate. One well-maintained client library gives retries, timeouts and metrics with no proxy hop, no control plane and no new failure mode.

  • Do not configure retries and timeouts at both the gateway and the mesh. Two retrying layers multiply load on a failing backend, and mismatched timeouts make the outer hop blame the wrong component.

  • Scale limit worth naming: the ceiling is configuration propagation — route count for a gateway, (config × proxy count) for a mesh — not request throughput. It presents as manifests that are applied but not yet in effect.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Ingress, Gateway API and a service mesh are three competing choices."

✅ Reality: Ingress and Gateway API are the same layer, one succeeding the other. A mesh is a different layer handling traffic that never reaches the edge. The real choice is Ingress-or-Gateway for north-south, and mesh-or-libraries for east-west.

❌ Misconception: "A service mesh gives you zero-trust security."

✅ Reality: It gives mTLS and workload identity — transport authentication. Authorization policy, secret management and human access are still yours. Encrypted traffic between two services that should not be talking is still traffic that should not be happening, which is why NetworkPolicy sits underneath (Item 143).

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "An Ingress resource routes traffic."

✅ Reality: It is inert configuration. Without a controller installed and watching, an Ingress object applies successfully and does nothing at all — no error, no event, no traffic. The controller is the thing that routes, and the resource is just a request written down.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Treating the three as alternatives. Naming the direction each handles — north-south versus east-west — reframes the question correctly and forecloses the muddle. It is the fastest way to show you have operated these rather than compared feature lists.

Justifying a mesh with observability. It is the weakest argument and a reviewer will push on it, because tracing and RED metrics are available from a gateway, from libraries and from eBPF tooling without a proxy in every request path. mTLS and gRPC balancing are the arguments that hold.

Not knowing that an Ingress does nothing without a controller. It is a small fact with a large diagnostic payoff, and it is the answer to a surprisingly common "I applied it and nothing happened".

Configuring the same responsibility twice. Retries at the gateway and in the mesh, TLS terminated at three hops, two timeout hierarchies. Saying "one owner per responsibility" unprompted signals you have debugged a multiplied retry storm.

Stopping at steady state. The interesting failures are in propagation and reload behaviour — config applied but not in effect, and long-lived connections reset by an unrelated team's deploy. Neither appears in request-path metrics.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Ingress in-spec routing Host and path only Everything else is per-controller annotations Kubernetes: Ingress
Gateway API resource roles 3 — GatewayClass, Gateway, Route The role split is the API's central design choice Gateway API: Introduction
Mesh proxy hops per call 2 (client sidecar + server sidecar) Loopback each; material only on very fast calls Istio: Sidecar or ambient?
Gateway config scaling ∝ total routes in the cluster One proxy config compiled from every Route Kubernetes: Ingress Controllers
Mesh config scaling ∝ config size × proxy count The reason ambient mode exists Istio: Sidecar or ambient?
Ingress resource without a controller No effect at all Applies cleanly, routes nothing Kubernetes: Ingress Controllers

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A gateway hop is one proxy; a mesh adds two per call. Both are sub-millisecond and both matter only on very fast calls
💰 Cost A mesh's per-pod proxy is a fleet-sized line item at a thousand pods — the motivation for ambient mode
🔒 Security / visibility The mesh supplies mTLS and identity; the gateway supplies edge authn and rate limiting; neither replaces NetworkPolicy
📈 Scale Configuration propagation is the ceiling, not throughput — and it fails as "applied but not in effect"
🔧 Ops complexity Three layers with overlapping capabilities; the discipline is one owner per responsibility, enforced by review
🐛 Debuggability A request may cross four proxies; without consistent trace propagation, locating the hop that failed is guesswork

16. Real World Usage

Gateway API's role split is the feature driving adoption, more than any routing capability. Platform teams wanted a way to own TLS and listeners without owning every team's routes, and Ingress had no boundary to draw — which is why the migration argument in practice is organisational rather than technical.

Ambient mode exists because sidecar cost is real. Istio's shift to a per-node data plane with optional per-namespace L7 proxies is a direct response to the per-pod overhead multiplied across large clusters, and it is the strongest signal available that the sidecar model had a scaling problem rather than merely a complexity one.

The reloading-controller connection-reset problem is why Envoy-based controllers won at scale. Clusters serving WebSocket or SSE discovered that any team's route change disconnected their users, and the fix — incremental xDS rather than process reload — is now the default expectation for a production ingress tier.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • xDS — the family of discovery service APIs (listener, route, cluster, endpoint) that a control plane uses to push configuration into Envoy incrementally. Decoding it explains the scaling difference in this note: xDS updates a running proxy in place, where a reload restarts it and drops connections.

  • mTLS — mutual TLS: both sides present certificates, so the server authenticates the client as well as the reverse. It is what turns a mesh's encryption into workload identity rather than just confidentiality.

  • 146-gpu-inference-load-balancing.md — where per-request routing becomes a cost decision

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • A cloud L7 balancer per Service — managed, but routing lives outside the cluster's API

  • Client libraries — east-west policy without a proxy, viable for a single-language estate

  • eBPF-based L7 policy — emerging alternative to sidecars for some mesh functions

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • NetworkPolicy — the layer beneath; a mesh authorizes, but the flat network still routes (Item 143)

  • Headless Services — how a gateway or sidecar addresses pods individually (Item 140)

  • Probes and draining — what makes route changes and rollouts non-disruptive (Items 144, 145)

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Usually as "how does traffic get into your cluster, and how do services talk to each other?" — two questions that people answer as one. The strong answer separates them by direction, assigns each responsibility to exactly one hop, and justifies the mesh with a requirement rather than with capability. On an AI platform the follow-up is invariably the streaming path, where a buffering default at any hop destroys the product metric.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (hundreds of routes, ~200 pods) Gateway config generation time; sidecar memory becomes visible xDS-based controller; ambient mode for the mesh
100× (thousands of routes, thousands of pods) Control-plane fan-out: config × proxy count; propagation delay Scope config per proxy; ambient; split very large clusters
1000× (multi-cluster) One control plane is a single failure domain for all routing Cluster-per-region with federated gateways; independent control planes

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: reload behaviour. A reloading controller resets long-lived connections on any team's route change.

  • 100×: config propagation. Manifests applied and not yet in effect, inconsistently across pods — correct everywhere, working nowhere.

  • Operational: the same responsibility configured at two layers — retries most often — discovered only when a struggling backend receives nine attempts per request.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Config propagation latency — reload duration or xDS push p99. The number behind the most confusing incidents in this area.

  • Connection resets correlated with deploys of other teams' resources. The reloading-controller signature.

  • Client-measured time-to-first-token on streaming routes. Every hop here can destroy it and no server-side metric will show it.

  • Per-pod request distribution on gRPC and inference paths. Confirms per-request routing is actually in force rather than assumed.

notes.title: CoreDNS & In-Cluster Service Discovery

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Walk me through what a pod's resolver does with api.example.com.
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
CoreDNS replicas, node-local cache, or autopath?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The record scheme and the search-path behaviour — Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods

  • The plugin that serves cluster records — CoreDNS: kubernetes plugin

  • Removing the search-path amplification server-side — CoreDNS: autopath plugin

  • Bonus — Kubernetes: Debugging DNS Resolution

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is ndots:5 and why does it hurt? Names with fewer than 5 dots try every search domain first — up to 5 lookups before the right one.
How many queries for api.example.com from a pod? Typically 5+ (4 search-domain misses, then the absolute name), doubled for A and AAAA.
The fully-qualified in-cluster name? <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
The cheapest fix for external-name latency? A trailing dot — api.example.com. — or ndots:1 via dnsConfig.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

CoreDNS is the cluster's resolver, serving records for Services and pods and forwarding everything else upstream. The pathology worth knowing is the search path: pods are configured with ndots:5 and four search domains, so any name with fewer than five dots — which is every external hostname — is tried against each search domain first. Resolving api.example.com costs five queries instead of one, doubled if the client asks for A and AAAA. That is a latency tax on every external call and a multiplier on CoreDNS load, and the fixes are a trailing dot, ndots:1, or a node-local DNS cache.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through what a pod's resolver does with api.example.com.

The pod's /etc/resolv.conf contains the cluster DNS address, a search list — typically <namespace>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local and the node's own domain — and options ndots:5. The ndots value means: if the queried name contains fewer than five dots, treat it as relative and try appending each search domain before trying the name as absolute.

api.example.com has two dots, so the resolver issues api.example.com.default.svc.cluster.local (NXDOMAIN), then api.example.com.svc.cluster.local (NXDOMAIN), then api.example.com.cluster.local (NXDOMAIN), then the node domain variant (NXDOMAIN), and only then api.example.com itself. Five queries where one was needed — and most clients request A and AAAA records concurrently, so it is ten packets to CoreDNS for one name.

The reason ndots:5 exists at all is to make short in-cluster names work: orders must expand to orders.default.svc.cluster.local, and orders.other-ns must expand too. Setting ndots:1 fixes external lookups and breaks those short forms, which is why the safer per-workload fix is a trailing dot on external hostnames — api.example.com. is already absolute, so the search path is skipped entirely.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

CoreDNS replicas, node-local cache, or autopath?

🎯 Really testing: whether you fix the amplification or just add capacity to absorb it.

Scaling CoreDNS replicas is the reflex and the weakest option: it absorbs the load without reducing it, every pod still pays five round trips per external name, and the latency tax remains. It is worth doing as a floor — CoreDNS should never be a two-replica single point of contention — but it treats the symptom.

NodeLocal DNSCache puts a caching resolver on every node, so pod queries hit loopback rather than crossing the network to a CoreDNS pod. It collapses the latency of the four NXDOMAIN misses to near zero, removes most CoreDNS load, and — on VPC-native clusters — also relieves pressure on the per-interface query limit toward the cloud resolver (Section 12, Item 133). It is the highest-return infrastructure change here.

autopath is the server-side fix: CoreDNS recognises the search-path pattern and returns the correct answer on the first query, eliminating the extra round trips at the source rather than caching them. It reduces query volume genuinely rather than absorbing it, at the cost of CoreDNS needing to watch pods, which adds memory and API load.

My order: NodeLocal DNSCache first because it helps every query type and is operationally simple; a trailing dot or ndots:2 on the workloads making heavy external calls; autopath when CoreDNS query volume is still the constraint. And regardless of all three, client-side connection reuse removes the lookups entirely — a service that opens one pooled connection per destination resolves once, not once per request.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Fix Removes queries or absorbs them? Blast radius Effort When you'd actually pick it
More CoreDNS replicas Absorbs Cluster-wide Trivial A floor, not a fix
NodeLocal DNSCache Absorbs, at ~zero latency Per node Moderate (a DaemonSet) The default first move at any real scale
Trailing dot on external names Removes One workload Trivial, but per-call-site Heavy external callers you control
ndots:2 via dnsConfig Removes One workload Trivial Same, without editing every hostname
autopath in CoreDNS Removes Cluster-wide Moderate; CoreDNS watches pods Query volume is the constraint
Connection pooling in clients Removes entirely One workload Application change Always worth doing anyway

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The amplification factor is (search domains + 1) × address families. With four search domains and dual-stack clients that is ten queries per external name — so a service making 1,000 external calls per second with no connection reuse generates 10,000 queries per second against CoreDNS for names it already knows. That is the mechanism behind "CoreDNS is our bottleneck", and it is an amplification problem rather than a capacity one.

In-cluster names pay the tax too, just less. orders has zero dots, so it hits the first search domain and resolves immediately — one query. orders.other-ns has one dot and also resolves on the first or second try. It is specifically external names, which always have two or more dots and never match a search domain, that pay the full penalty.

The per-interface query limit compounds it. On cloud clusters, queries that CoreDNS forwards upstream go to the VPC resolver, which enforces a packets-per-second cap per network interface (Section 12, Item 133). Search-path amplification multiplies the traffic hitting that cap, so DNS failures under load can come from the cloud resolver rather than from CoreDNS — and the symptom, intermittent resolution errors correlated with traffic, looks identical.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not set ndots:1 cluster-wide without checking short names. It fixes external lookups and breaks every workload relying on orders or orders.other-ns expanding through the search path — a broad change with a narrow benefit.

  • Do not scale CoreDNS replicas as the answer. It absorbs amplified load without reducing it; the per-query latency tax on every external call remains exactly the same.

  • Do not ignore client-side DNS caching behaviour. A client that never re-resolves keeps dialling dead pods behind a headless Service; one that resolves per request generates the amplification described above. Both extremes are wrong.

  • Do not treat CoreDNS as stateless capacity. It watches the API server for Services and EndpointSlices, so its memory scales with cluster object count, and a large cluster's CoreDNS is sized by object count as much as by query rate.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "DNS latency in Kubernetes means CoreDNS is slow."

✅ Reality: CoreDNS usually answers in well under a millisecond. The latency is the four NXDOMAIN round trips the resolver makes before trying the name you asked for, caused by ndots:5 and the search path. Adding CoreDNS capacity does not shorten that sequence.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The search path only affects names that fail to resolve."

✅ Reality: It affects every external name, all of which resolve perfectly — just after four unnecessary NXDOMAINs first. The successful lookup is the fifth query, so the cost is invisible in success metrics and shows up only as latency and CoreDNS load.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 04-dns/30-dns-resolution.md — recursive resolution and the search-path mechanism generally

  • 139-services-and-kube-proxy.md — the Service names CoreDNS is resolving

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 140-headless-services-statefulset-dns.md — where DNS is the load balancing mechanism

  • Section 12 133-private-dns-cloud.md — the cloud resolver CoreDNS forwards to, and its query limit

  • 04-dns/32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md — why client caching decides whether any of this matters

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
How does "isolation" actually get switched on?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
NetworkPolicy, mesh authorization policy, or both?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Semantics, the default-allow reality and the isolation rule — Kubernetes: Network Policies

  • A worked default-deny example — Kubernetes: Declare Network Policy

  • Identity-based enforcement rather than address-based — Cilium: Kubernetes Without kube-proxy

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is the default with no policies? All pods can reach all pods. The flat model mandates it — isolation is opt-in.
What happens when one policy selects a pod? That pod becomes isolated for that direction; only what policies allow gets through.
Are policies allow or deny? Allow only. The effective rule is the union of every policy selecting the pod.
What if the CNI doesn't support them? The manifest applies successfully and enforces nothing. No error, no event.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Kubernetes' networking model mandates that every pod can reach every pod, so a cluster with no NetworkPolicy has zero east-west isolation — that is the specified default, not a misconfiguration. A NetworkPolicy changes that selectively: the moment any policy selects a pod for a direction, that pod becomes isolated in that direction and only explicitly allowed traffic passes. Policies are allow-only and additive, so you get default-deny by applying an empty-ingress policy per namespace and then adding allows. The trap is that enforcement is the CNI's job — Flannel accepts the manifests and enforces nothing at all.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How does "isolation" actually get switched on?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that policies are additive allows with an implicit switch, not a firewall rule list.

A pod is non-isolated until some policy selects it. Once any policy with an Ingress section selects a pod, that pod is isolated for ingress: all inbound traffic is dropped except what the union of selecting policies allows. Egress works the same way independently — a pod can be isolated for ingress and wide open for egress, or the reverse, depending on which sections appear in the policies that select it.

That is why default-deny is expressed as a policy with an empty ingress rule set: it selects every pod in the namespace, declares policyTypes: [Ingress], and permits nothing. It flips the switch without allowing anything, and every subsequent policy adds a permitted flow. There is no deny primitive at all, so you cannot write "allow everything except X" — you enumerate what is allowed, which is the same allow-only model as a security group (Section 12, Item 126).

Two subtleties that come up. Selectors are identity-like: podSelector and namespaceSelector match labels, so policy survives pod churn and rescheduling in a way address-based rules cannot. And policies are namespaced: a policy in namespace A cannot constrain traffic between two pods in namespace B, so default-deny has to be applied per namespace — which is why it belongs in namespace provisioning automation rather than in each team's manifests.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

NetworkPolicy, mesh authorization policy, or both?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know they operate at different layers and what each cannot see.

NetworkPolicy is L3/L4: it decides whether a connection between two pods may exist, based on labels, namespaces and ports. It is enforced by the CNI in the kernel, applies to all traffic regardless of protocol, and costs nothing at request time. What it cannot do is see inside a request — no paths, no methods, no headers — and it authorises the pod, not a verified identity.

Mesh authorization policy is L7 and identity-based: it decides whether a workload with a cryptographically verified identity may call a specific path or method. That is genuinely stronger, and it is also only enforced by the sidecar — so it governs traffic that goes through the proxy and nothing else. A pod that bypasses its sidecar, or a protocol the mesh does not parse, is unconstrained by it.

The two compose rather than compete, and the composition is the answer: NetworkPolicy as the floor, so a connection cannot even be established between workloads that have no business talking; mesh policy on top for path- and method-level rules with verified identity. Running only the mesh leaves the flat network underneath fully open to anything that sidesteps the proxy; running only NetworkPolicy gives you coarse connectivity control with no request-level granularity. For a multi-tenant cluster I would insist on the NetworkPolicy floor first, because it is free, protocol-agnostic and does not depend on a proxy being in the path.

4. Quick Comparison Table

NetworkPolicy Mesh authorization policy Security group (Section 12)
Layer L3/L4 L7 L3/L4
Selects by Pod and namespace labels Verified workload identity Security group membership
Granularity Pod, port, protocol Path, method, header, identity Instance/ENI, port
Enforced by The CNI, in kernel The sidecar proxy The cloud fabric
Bypassable No Yes, if traffic avoids the proxy No
Deny rules None — allow-only Yes None — allow-only
Reaches inside a node Yes Yes No — stops at the node interface
When you'd actually pick it Always, as the floor Path-level rules with verified identity Node-level and non-cluster workloads

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The isolation switch is the mechanism people misread. Policies do not deny; they flip a pod into isolated mode for a direction and then enumerate what is permitted. So adding a policy that allows one flow also blocks every other flow to that pod, which is a much larger change than the manifest looks — and it is the reason a first NetworkPolicy in a namespace frequently breaks something unrelated.

Denied traffic is dropped silently. There is no RST and no ICMP unreachable, so a blocked client sees a connection timeout rather than a refusal. That distinction is the diagnostic: connection refused means nothing is listening, connection hangs then times out is the signature of a policy drop, and it is the fastest way to tell the two apart under pressure.

Enforcement is CNI-dependent, and the failure is silent. The API server accepts and stores NetworkPolicy objects regardless of whether anything enforces them, so on a Flannel cluster kubectl get networkpolicy shows a tidy default-deny that does nothing whatsoever. The only way to know is to test the drop — which is why a policy test in CI is worth more here than in most places.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not assume policies are enforced because they applied. Confirm the CNI supports them, then verify by actually attempting a connection that should be blocked. A green kubectl apply proves nothing.

  • Do not add a first policy to a busy namespace without checking what it isolates. Selecting a pod switches on isolation for that direction entirely, so a policy meant to allow one flow silently blocks every other inbound flow to those pods.

  • Do not rely on mesh authorization alone in a multi-tenant cluster. It governs traffic through the proxy; the flat network underneath still routes everything else. NetworkPolicy is the floor precisely because it cannot be bypassed by avoiding a sidecar.

  • Do not write policies against IP ranges where labels will do. Pod addresses churn constantly, so ipBlock rules go stale or over-permit; label selectors are the identity-like formulation that stays true.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Kubernetes namespaces provide network isolation."

✅ Reality: A namespace is an API-level scoping and RBAC boundary. It has no effect on the network at all — pods in different namespaces reach each other freely unless a NetworkPolicy says otherwise, and most clusters have none.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "A NetworkPolicy that allows traffic from the frontend is purely additive — it can't break anything."

✅ Reality: Selecting a pod switches on isolation for that direction, so the policy simultaneously blocks every other inbound source to those pods. The first policy applied to a namespace is the most dangerous one, and it usually breaks a monitoring scrape or a health check nobody was thinking about.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 137-k8s-networking-model.md — the flat, fully-reachable default this exists to constrain

  • 138-cni-plugins.md — the component that does or does not enforce these

  • Section 12 126-security-groups-vs-nacls.md — the same allow-only model at the cloud layer

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 141-ingress-gateway-mesh.md — mesh authorization as the L7 layer above this one

  • Section 12 136-network-security-posture.md — where cluster policy fits the wider posture

  • Agent sandboxing in the Agentic folder — pod-level egress control for model-directed traffic

notes.title: Probes vs Load Balancer Health Checks

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
What should each probe actually check?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
The load balancer and Kubernetes both health-check. How should they interact during a rollout?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The three probe types and their distinct consequences — Kubernetes: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

  • How probe state moves into endpoints — Kubernetes: Explore Termination Behavior for Pods and Their Endpoints

  • The external half of the loop — AWS: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups

  • Bonus — Amazon Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Liveness vs readiness — the consequence? Liveness failure restarts the container. Readiness failure only removes it from endpoints.
What is a startup probe for? Slow starts — it suppresses the other two until it passes, so nothing kills a warming pod.
Why do two health-check systems exist? Kubernetes gates endpoints; the cloud LB gates nodes or targets. They run independently.
The dangerous probe mistake? Pointing liveness at a shared dependency — a blip restarts the whole fleet.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Kubernetes has three probes with three different consequences: startup suppresses the others while a slow pod warms, readiness gates whether the pod appears in EndpointSlices, and liveness restarts the container when it fails. Independently, a cloud load balancer runs its own health check against whatever it targets. The two systems do not know about each other, so during a rollout they can disagree — Kubernetes has removed a pod from endpoints while the load balancer still considers its node healthy, or vice versa. The dangerous mistake is a deep liveness probe: a shared dependency blip then restarts every pod at once.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What should each probe actually check?

🎯 Really testing: whether you scope probes by their consequence rather than by their name.

Liveness answers "is this process wedged beyond recovery?" and its failure costs a restart, discarding warm caches and in-flight requests. So it should be shallow and slow: a static endpoint that proves the HTTP stack responds, with a generous failure threshold. Anything deeper turns a dependency problem into a crash loop.

Readiness answers "can this instance serve right now?" and its failure only removes the pod from endpoints, which is cheap and reversible. So it can be deeper — connection pool initialised, config loaded, model weights in memory — but it must stay local to the instance. Checking a shared database here means every pod fails simultaneously when that database blips, and the Service ends up with zero endpoints: a total outage caused by a partial degradation (Section 11, Item 112).

Startup answers "is it still warming up?" and exists because the other two need different timing during initialisation. It suppresses liveness and readiness until it passes, with a failure budget sized to the genuine worst-case start — three minutes for a model server loading weights. Without it, you must either set a liveness threshold so loose it never catches a real hang, or watch pods get killed for booting slowly.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

The load balancer and Kubernetes both health-check. How should they interact during a rollout?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up whenever someone reports 502s during deploys that nothing explains.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can reason about two independent control loops with different periods.

They interact badly by default, because they run on different clocks. Kubernetes notices a pod terminating within a second or two and removes it from EndpointSlices; a cloud load balancer with a 30-second interval and a threshold of two takes up to 90 seconds to notice anything (Section 11, Item 112). If the load balancer targets nodes, a node whose only pod for that Service has just terminated keeps receiving traffic that now has nowhere to go — 502s that correlate with deploys and appear in no application log.

Two structural fixes. Target pod IPs rather than nodes, so the load balancer's target set tracks EndpointSlices directly and deregistration follows readiness. And make the pod's shutdown sequence outlast the slower loop: fail readiness first, keep serving through a preStop sleep long enough for both endpoint propagation and the load balancer's deregistration delay, then exit (Item 145).

My rule: IP-target mode wherever the controller supports it, a preStop sleep sized to the load balancer's detection window rather than to Kubernetes', and terminationGracePeriodSeconds comfortably longer than that sleep plus the longest in-flight request. The failure to avoid is tuning only the Kubernetes side and concluding the cloud load balancer is broken.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Startup probe Readiness probe Liveness probe Cloud LB health check
Failure consequence Eventually restarts the container Removed from EndpointSlices Restarts the container Target deregistered
Reversible? n/a Yes, instantly No — warm state is lost Yes
Depth Whatever proves warm-up finished Deep, but local only Shallow and slow Whatever endpoint you point it at
Typical timing Generous budget (minutes) 5 s interval, fast out 20 s+ interval, slow to fire 30 s interval by default
Knows about the others Suppresses the other two No No No — entirely independent
When it bites Absent on a slow-starting pod Checking a shared dependency Checking anything deep Slower than Kubernetes during rollouts

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Detection latency is interval × threshold on each side, independently. Kubernetes with a 5-second readiness interval and threshold 2 reacts in ~10 seconds; an ALB at its 30-second default with threshold 2 takes up to ~90. The gap between those two numbers is the window in which the two systems disagree, and it is where rollout 502s live.

The consequences are asymmetric, which is why depth must differ. A readiness failure removes one pod from a set and is undone the moment the check passes again — cheap enough to be sensitive. A liveness failure destroys the container: warm caches gone, in-flight requests dropped, and for a model server a multi-minute reload. Sensitivity that is appropriate for readiness is destructive for liveness, and the single most common outage in this area is a deep liveness probe restarting an entire fleet when a shared dependency slows down.

A startup probe changes the arithmetic rather than the checks. Its failure budget must exceed the genuine worst-case start; a model server taking three minutes needs roughly 200 seconds of budget, and the metric that tells you whether the budget is honest is time-from-container-start to first successful request, drifting upward release by release.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not point a liveness probe at anything but the process itself. A dependency check here converts a degradation into a fleet-wide crash loop, discarding every warm cache simultaneously and then hammering the recovering dependency with cold starts.

  • Do not check shared dependencies in readiness either. Every pod fails at once and the Service drops to zero endpoints — a total outage from a partial problem. Readiness should be deep about this instance and blind to everything shared.

  • Do not tune only the Kubernetes side of a rollout. The cloud load balancer runs its own slower loop; if the pod exits on Kubernetes' timeline, traffic still arriving from the load balancer hits a closed socket.

  • Do not omit a startup probe on slow-starting workloads. Without it you must choose between a liveness threshold too loose to catch real hangs and one that kills pods for booting normally.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Liveness and readiness are the same check with different names."

✅ Reality: One restarts the container, the other only removes it from a list. Pointing both at the same deep endpoint means a slow dependency does not merely take pods out of rotation — it kills and restarts them, turning a recoverable degradation into a cluster-wide cold start.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "If readiness fails, the load balancer stops sending traffic."

✅ Reality: Kubernetes stops sending traffic. A cloud load balancer targeting nodes has no idea readiness failed and keeps forwarding on its own schedule until its own health check notices — up to 90 seconds later on ALB defaults. Two independent loops, and only one of them read your manifest.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • Section 11 112-health-checks.md — health checking as a general availability control, including fail-open

  • 139-services-and-kube-proxy.md — EndpointSlices, which readiness gates membership in

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 145-rollouts-connection-handling.md — the shutdown sequence these probes drive

  • 146-gpu-inference-load-balancing.md — why slow-starting GPU pods need all three probes

  • Section 11 113-outlier-detection-circuit-breaking.md — passive detection, which reacts far faster than either loop here

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Walk me through pod termination and say where requests get dropped.
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
How do you drain a fleet of long-lived WebSocket or SSE connections?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The termination sequence, step by step — Kubernetes: Pod Lifecycle

  • What actually happens to endpoints while a pod terminates — Kubernetes: Explore Termination Behavior for Pods and Their Endpoints

  • preStop and the hook contract — Kubernetes: Container Lifecycle Hooks

  • Bonus — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What happens concurrently at pod deletion? Endpoint removal and SIGTERM — not in order. That race is the whole problem.
What is preStop actually for? Buying time: sleep while endpoint removal propagates, before the process stops accepting.
What ends the grace period abruptly? terminationGracePeriodSeconds expiring → SIGKILL, mid-drain.
Why are long-lived connections worse? Draining must outlast the connection, not the request — a 10-minute stream needs 10 minutes.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

When a pod is deleted, two things happen at the same time: the endpoints controller starts removing it from EndpointSlices, and the kubelet sends SIGTERM. If the application exits promptly on SIGTERM, it stops accepting connections while traffic is still being routed to it — because propagation to every kube-proxy, every ingress controller and every cloud load balancer takes seconds. The fix is a preStop sleep that keeps the pod serving until propagation finishes, and a grace period longer than that sleep plus the longest in-flight work. For WebSocket, gRPC and SSE the arithmetic changes: you are draining connections, not requests.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through pod termination and say where requests get dropped.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the race is concurrent rather than sequential.

On deletion the API server marks the pod terminating, and two independent things start. The endpoints controller updates EndpointSlices to mark the pod not-ready, which then has to reach every kube-proxy on every node, every ingress controller, every mesh sidecar and — slowest of all — any cloud load balancer targeting it. Simultaneously the kubelet runs preStop if defined, then sends SIGTERM.

Requests are dropped in the window between "the process stopped accepting" and "everything has stopped sending". A well-behaved application that closes its listener on SIGTERM does exactly the wrong thing here: it is now refusing connections that the dataplane is still routing to it, and the client sees a connection reset rather than a clean response. The volume is small but non-zero, and it is exactly the class of error people describe as "a few 502s on every deploy" and then stop investigating.

The correct sequence therefore inverts intuition: keep serving after SIGTERM. preStop sleeps long enough for propagation, during which the pod continues answering normally; only then does the application begin its shutdown, finishing in-flight work before exiting. The pod is deliberately alive and serving while Kubernetes considers it terminating, and that overlap is the whole mechanism.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How do you drain a fleet of long-lived WebSocket or SSE connections?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up on any streaming product's deploy story.

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice that connection lifetime, not request duration, sets the grace period.

For request/response traffic, draining is bounded by the longest in-flight request — usually seconds, so a 30-second grace period covers it. For long-lived connections it is bounded by the connection, which may last as long as a user keeps a tab open. Setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds to the maximum connection lifetime is not viable: deploys would take hours, and SIGKILL at the end still cuts whatever remains.

So the honest answer is that long-lived connections cannot be drained passively; they must be actively closed with a signal the client understands. For gRPC that is GOAWAY, which tells the client to finish open streams and reconnect — it re-resolves, lands on a new pod, and nothing is lost. For SSE, closing the stream cleanly lets EventSource reconnect on its own with Last-Event-ID, which is exactly what the protocol's reconnect semantics exist for. For WebSocket it is a close frame with a code the client treats as retryable.

The design implication is that the client's reconnect behaviour is part of your deploy strategy, not an application detail. My rule: preStop that first stops accepting new connections and signals existing ones to reconnect, a grace period sized to let that reconnection wave complete rather than to outlast the connections, and a surge-limited rollout so the wave hits a fleet that still has capacity. A deploy that is invisible to users is one where every client reconnected quickly, not one where no connection was ever closed.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Traffic shape Drain bounded by Grace period Mechanism Failure if you get it wrong
HTTP/1.1 request/response Longest in-flight request ~30 s preStop sleep, then finish and exit A few resets per deploy
HTTP/2 or gRPC Open streams after GOAWAY 30–60 s GOAWAY, client re-resolves Requests fail mid-stream; client may not retry
SSE Client reconnect time 30–60 s Close cleanly; EventSource reconnects Stream truncated with a 200 — looks like success
WebSocket Client reconnect time 30–60 s Close frame with a retryable code Abrupt disconnect, application-visible
Batch or long jobs Job completion Job-length Drain, or checkpoint and resume SIGKILL mid-work, partial results

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The grace period must exceed the sum, not the maximum. It has to cover preStop duration + the longest in-flight work after SIGTERM. A 20-second preStop with a 30-second grace leaves only 10 seconds to finish real work, and SIGKILL at 30 undoes the careful shutdown entirely — the most common misconfiguration in this note, because both numbers look reasonable in isolation.

preStop duration must exceed the slowest consumer of endpoint state. Kubernetes propagation is typically a few seconds; a cloud load balancer with a 30-second check interval and threshold 2 is up to 90. So a preStop tuned to Kubernetes' timeline still drops traffic arriving from the load balancer, which is why IP-target mode — where deregistration follows EndpointSlices directly — matters more than any sleep value (Item 144).

Reconnection is a thundering-herd problem. Closing n connections at once produces n simultaneous reconnects, TLS handshakes and DNS lookups against a fleet that is one pod smaller. A surge-limited rollout with maxUnavailable low and a pause between batches spreads that wave; without it, a deploy can knock over the very fleet it is updating.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not exit immediately on SIGTERM. It is the intuitive, well-behaved thing to do and it is wrong here: the dataplane is still routing to you. Serve through a preStop sleep first.

  • Do not set terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than preStop plus real drain time. SIGKILL mid-drain is indistinguishable from having no drain at all, and it is easy to reach by treating the two numbers separately.

  • Do not attempt to passively outlast long-lived connections. Sizing the grace period to a WebSocket's lifetime makes deploys unbounded and still ends in SIGKILL. Close them actively with a signal the client retries on.

  • Do not roll out streaming workloads without surge limits. Every replaced pod produces a reconnection wave, and replacing several at once concentrates the herd on a shrinking fleet.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service before sending SIGTERM."

✅ Reality: They happen concurrently. There is no ordering guarantee at all, and the propagation of endpoint removal to every dataplane and cloud load balancer takes seconds longer than SIGTERM takes to arrive. Every drop during a deploy comes from that gap.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "A graceful shutdown handler in the application is enough for zero-downtime deploys."

✅ Reality: A perfect SIGTERM handler still drops requests, because the problem is not how the process shuts down but when it stops accepting relative to when traffic stops arriving. Without a preStop sleep covering propagation, the most careful shutdown code in the world closes the listener too early.

🧭 Scope. This folder owns the wire: which pod a request reaches and why. Model-serving internals — batching, KV-cache mechanics, GPU utilisation — belong to the LLM serving folder per the index's cross-reference block, and are pointed to rather than explained here.

📚 Reference Links

  • The Kubernetes-native answer to inference routing — Gateway API Inference Extension: Introduction

  • The routing abstraction it adds — Gateway API Inference Extension: InferencePool

  • The algorithms available once routing is per request — Envoy: Supported load balancers

  • Bonus — Kubernetes: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why is round robin wrong here? It counts turns. Generation cost varies by orders of magnitude, so turns ≠ work.
What is the minimum correct algorithm? Least request (in-flight requests), ideally with power-of-two-choices.
What does a ClusterIP do to this? Pins every request on a connection to one pod — no algorithm can recover from that.
What signal beats in-flight count? The server's own queue depth or KV-cache occupancy, reported back to the router.
The metric that detects all of this? Max-to-median in-flight requests per pod. Nothing else shows it.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Inference requests differ in cost by orders of magnitude — a twenty-token reply and a two-thousand-token generation are the same "one request" to a round-robin balancer. So turn-order balancing forms queues on unlucky pods while others idle, and the expensive resource sits underused. The minimum correct answer is least request with power-of-two-choices, which keeps a pod out of rotation while it is busy. Above that, the router can use signals only the model server knows — queue depth, KV-cache occupancy — which is what the Gateway API Inference Extension standardises. And none of it works through a ClusterIP, because that pins per connection.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why does request-cost variance break round robin specifically?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can connect variance to queueing rather than to fairness.

Round robin is fair in turns: over n requests each pod receives n/k. That is only the same as fair in work when requests cost roughly the same. Queueing theory is explicit about what happens otherwise — mean queue length grows with the variance of service time, so at identical throughput a high-variance workload produces far longer waits than a uniform one.

Concretely: a pod midway through a 2,000-token generation is occupied for eight seconds. Round robin hands it the next request anyway when its turn comes, and that request waits behind eight seconds of work while another pod idles. Average utilisation looks healthy, p50 looks fine, and p99 is dominated by requests queued behind long generations.

Least request fixes the mechanism: a busy pod is less attractive than an idle one, so work accumulates at the router — visible and drainable — rather than inside one worker. That is worth more than horizontal scaling, because scaling adds capacity while distribution decides whether the capacity is used.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Least request, or routing on model-server-reported signals?

📍 Seen in the wild: the current live question in inference platform design.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know what in-flight count still fails to capture, and whether you can justify the extra machinery.

Least request treats every in-flight request as equal, which is better than treating every turn as equal but still wrong in two ways for generation workloads. First, a request that has emitted 1,900 of 2,000 tokens is nearly done, while one that just started is not — both count as one. Second, and more importantly, modern servers batch continuously: admitting one more request to a pod with spare KV-cache capacity may cost almost nothing, while admitting it to a pod near cache saturation causes eviction or queueing that hurts every request already there. In-flight count cannot see either.

Routing on server-reported signals — queue depth, KV-cache utilisation, admitted batch size — captures both, because the model server is the only component that knows them. That is what the Gateway API Inference Extension formalises: an endpoint picker that consumes metrics from the pool's pods and chooses per request, sitting behind a normal Gateway. Prefix-aware variants go further and route requests sharing a prompt prefix to the pod that already has it cached.

My position: least request with P2C plus slow start is the floor and it is a config change — take it first, always. Server-signal routing earns its machinery when generation lengths vary widely, when prefix reuse is high (a shared system prompt across tenants), or when the fleet is large enough that a few points of GPU utilisation pays for the component. It is not worth adopting to squeeze a well-balanced four-pod fleet.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Strategy Signal used Sees generation length? Sees cache state? Effort When you'd actually pick it
Round robin Turn order No No Default Never, for generation workloads
Least connections Open sockets No No Config Never here — HTTP/2 decouples it
Least request In-flight requests Partially No Config line The floor. Always at least this
+ Power-of-two-choices Sampled in-flight Partially No Config line Always — removes herding on empty pods
+ Slow start Time since ready n/a n/a Config line Always — cold GPU pods attract least-request traffic
Peak EWMA Recent latency × in-flight Indirectly Indirectly Config + tuning Pods degrade (thermal throttling) rather than fail
Server-reported queue depth Model server metrics Yes Partially A router component Wide length variance; large fleets
KV-cache / prefix aware Cache occupancy, prompt prefix Yes Yes A router component High prefix reuse; cache pressure is the bottleneck

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The prerequisite dominates every algorithm choice. Through a ClusterIP, kube-proxy decides once per connection, so a handful of gateway pods holding HTTP/2 connections pin every request to a handful of GPU pods: with c connections over n pods, at least n − c pods receive nothing, and at c = 5, n = 40 that is 87.5% of the fleet idle by construction (Section 11, Item 114). No algorithm recovers from that, because the algorithm is never consulted. Per-request routing requires addressing pods individually — a headless Service or an EndpointSlice-aware gateway.

Least request's residual error is what the extra signals address. In-flight count treats a nearly-finished generation and a just-started one identically, and it is blind to batch and cache state entirely. Queue depth captures admission pressure; KV-cache occupancy captures whether one more request is cheap or expensive on that pod. Both are known only to the model server, which is why the signal has to be reported rather than inferred — and why standardising that reporting is what the Inference Extension is for.

Slow start matters more here than anywhere else. A newly-ready pod has zero in-flight requests, making it maximally attractive at exactly the moment it is least able to serve. Without a ramp, every scale-out bursts at the coldest pod in the fleet. Pair it with a startup probe sized to the real load time (Item 144).

The detection metric is the same one as everywhere in this section. Max-to-median in-flight requests per pod: near 1.1 when routing works, 3 or more when the algorithm is wrong, effectively unbounded when a ClusterIP is pinning. Nothing else surfaces it — error rates are zero, health checks pass, and only GPU utilisation variance and the bill show the damage.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not tune the algorithm before removing per-connection pinning. If traffic reaches pods through a ClusterIP, the algorithm is not being consulted. Fix the addressing first; everything else is wasted effort.

  • Do not adopt server-signal routing for a small, uniform fleet. Least request with P2C is a config line and captures most of the benefit; an endpoint-picker component for four evenly-loaded pods is machinery without a return.

  • Do not use least request without slow start on GPU pods. Cold pods are maximally attractive at their least capable moment, and a cold GPU pod is minutes from useful rather than seconds.

  • Do not drain inference pods on a request-shaped timeline. A generation in flight may run for minutes, so the grace period and rollout strategy have to account for it (Item 145).

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Our GPUs are underutilised, so we need more efficient batching."

✅ Reality: Check distribution before efficiency. If max-to-median in-flight per pod is 3 or higher, the problem is that most pods are not receiving work — and no batching improvement helps a pod with nothing to batch. Serving efficiency is the LLM folder's subject; this one is the wire, and the wire is the cheaper fix.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Least request is enough for inference."

✅ Reality: It is the floor, not the ceiling. It cannot distinguish a request that is 95% complete from one that just started, and it is blind to KV-cache pressure — so a pod near cache saturation looks identical to an empty one with the same in-flight count. That gap is exactly why routing on server-reported signals became a standardised concern rather than a niche optimisation.
